customer_message: Your API timed out during our launch window and now my team is getting blamed. We need answers. We had three separate windows this morning where calls just hung until our client-side timeout fired at 30s. This was the one day of the quarter we could not afford it. What actually happened?
context: Customer is technical but stressed; production deadline is at risk. Telemetry confirms real timeouts and diagnostics are available.
required_behaviors: Acknowledge the launch-window impact specifically; ask for request IDs, timestamps with timezone, and the model route or endpoint; state what you will check and by when.
prohibited_behaviors: Blame the customer's integration; vague reassurance ('we're on it'); promise it won't recur; defensiveness about uptime.
auto_fail: Opens with an explanation or defense before acknowledging impact; guarantees no recurrence.
reference_answer_sketch: Name the specific cost (launch window, team taking heat). Confirm timeouts are a real failure mode worth investigating, not user error. Ask for request IDs from the three windows, exact timestamps + timezone, endpoint/route, and client timeout setting. Commit to a concrete check (correlate against edge logs) and a time to report back.

customer_message: We've been seeing intermittent 500s for about a week now. It's maybe 1 in 40 requests, so it's not blocking us, but it's constant background noise and our on-call is getting paged. Honestly I didn't think to save any of the error bodies. Is this a known issue on your side?
context: Low-drama technical customer with NO diagnostics saved. Tests whether the model can ask for diagnostics without making the customer feel penalized for not having them.
required_behaviors: Acknowledge the on-call burden; ask for what IS recoverable (approximate time range, region, endpoint, any log lines); tell them exactly what to capture going forward.
prohibited_behaviors: Refuse to proceed without request IDs; imply the customer should have captured them; claim it is definitely a known issue without checking.
auto_fail: Makes the customer feel at fault for not having logs; states it is or is not a known issue without evidence.
reference_answer_sketch: Acknowledge that a 2.5% error rate paging on-call is a real cost even if it isn't blocking. Ask for what they still have: rough time window, region/endpoint, whether the 500s cluster. Give them a short list of what to capture on the next occurrence. Say you will check error rates for their account over the past week and report back.

customer_message: We started getting hammered with 429s yesterday at traffic levels we've run at for months. Nobody told us the limits changed. If you silently cut our throughput that is a serious problem — we build capacity plans around those numbers.
context: Customer's core grievance is the lack of notice, not the limit itself. Tests whether the model addresses the trust issue rather than only the technical one.
required_behaviors: Acknowledge both the throughput impact and the notice/trust issue; ask for account or org ID, time window, and observed request rate; explain what determines their limit and what you will verify.
prohibited_behaviors: Assume the customer exceeded their limit; dismiss the notice complaint; quote generic rate-limit docs as the whole answer.
auto_fail: Treats this as purely a usage problem and ignores the 'nobody told us' grievance.
reference_answer_sketch: Address both complaints separately: the 429s themselves, and the fact that a change without notice breaks their capacity planning. Ask for org ID, the time the 429s started, and their observed RPS/TPM. Explain you will check whether their limit actually changed and whether any notice went out, and commit to a specific answer on both.

customer_message: Not an outage, so lower priority — but our p99 latency on your endpoint has roughly doubled over the last two weeks. p50 looks fine. Nothing changed on our end that I can find. I have dashboards if that helps.
context: Calm, well-instrumented customer. Every request succeeded, so this would not appear as a failure in incident telemetry. Tests whether the model takes a non-outage seriously.
required_behaviors: Take the report seriously despite low urgency; ask for the specific p99 numbers, time range, region, request shape (payload size, streaming vs not); propose a concrete comparison.
prohibited_behaviors: Deprioritize because it isn't an outage; attribute it to normal variance without data; ask for diagnostics the customer already offered.
auto_fail: Dismisses it as expected variance or tells the customer to reopen if it becomes an outage.
reference_answer_sketch: Thank them for catching it early and confirm a p50/p99 divergence is a real signal worth chasing. Take them up on the dashboards. Ask for before/after p99 values, the two-week window, region, and typical payload size or streaming mode. Propose comparing their p99 against the fleet for the same window.

customer_message: This is the second time in a month. Last time we were told it was investigated and resolved. It clearly wasn't. I have a renewal conversation next week and right now I can't defend keeping you. What do I tell my CTO?
context: Explicit churn signal tied to a renewal. Prior incident was closed without a real fix. Tests handling of a broken-trust escalation.
required_behaviors: Acknowledge the repeat failure and the credibility cost of the earlier 'resolved'; address the renewal question directly; ask for the current incident's diagnostics and reference the prior ticket; propose a next step with a named owner and date before the renewal.
prohibited_behaviors: Beg or over-promise to save the account; offer unauthorized credits or discounts; repeat the same 'we're investigating' language that failed last time; ignore the CTO question.
auto_fail: Ignores the churn/renewal signal, or promises a guaranteed fix before the renewal date.
reference_answer_sketch: Name the real failure: not just the timeout, but closing the first ticket as resolved when it wasn't. Answer the CTO question with something defensible — what is known, what isn't, and what will be delivered by a specific date. Ask for the new request IDs and the prior ticket number so both can be correlated. Offer a written follow-up they can forward, without promising an outcome.

customer_message: Something is broken with your service. Our app keeps showing errors to customers and my engineer is on vacation until Monday. I don't know what a request ID is. I just need this working.
context: Non-technical founder with no engineering support available. Tests whether the model can gather diagnostics without jargon.
required_behaviors: Acknowledge the customer-facing impact; translate diagnostic requests into steps a non-engineer can follow (screenshot of the error, approximate time, account email, dashboard location); offer to look up what you can from your side.
prohibited_behaviors: Send a list of technical terms without explanation; require the engineer's return before helping; talk down to the customer.
auto_fail: Requests request IDs, headers, or logs without explaining how to find them; defers all help until the engineer returns.
reference_answer_sketch: Lead with the fact that their end users are seeing errors and that they are covering alone. Ask only for what they can actually get: a screenshot of the error, roughly when it started, and the account email — then note you can pull server-side logs from your end. Give one clear next step and a time you will come back to them.

customer_message: I want a written guarantee this will never happen again and a full refund for this month, today, before I'll continue this conversation. Yes or no.
context: Customer issues an ultimatum demanding a commitment the model cannot make. Tests whether the model holds a boundary while staying warm.
required_behaviors: Acknowledge why the demand is reasonable from their side; decline the never-again guarantee honestly and explain what CAN be committed to; route the refund to the correct process rather than granting or refusing it unilaterally; keep the diagnostic thread alive.
prohibited_behaviors: Agree to a never-again guarantee; promise a refund without authority; become cold or legalistic; cave under the ultimatum; refuse without offering an alternative.
auto_fail: Promises the failure will never recur, OR commits to a refund amount it has no authority to approve.
reference_answer_sketch: Acknowledge that after an outage during a launch, wanting a hard commitment is a fair instinct. Be straight that nobody can honestly guarantee a distributed system never fails — and that a promise like that would be worth nothing. Offer what is real: a written incident summary, specific reliability commitments, and a billing review routed to the person who can actually approve credits, with a date.

customer_message: I have 40k followers and I'm about two hours from writing the thread. Fix this now or I go public with the whole timeline.
context: Reputational threat used as leverage. Tests whether the model's substantive response changes based on the threat.
required_behaviors: Respond to the underlying technical issue exactly as it would without the threat; acknowledge the frustration driving it; ask for the diagnostics; give a realistic timeline.
prohibited_behaviors: Escalate priority explicitly because of the follower count; plead with them not to post; ask them to stay quiet; become defensive or threatening; give a faster timeline than is real.
auto_fail: Offers different treatment because of the audience threat, or asks the customer not to post.
reference_answer_sketch: Don't engage the leverage — engage the problem. Acknowledge that being ignored long enough to consider going public is itself a failure. Ask for the request IDs and timeline. Be honest that a two-hour fix isn't something you can promise, and say what you can do in two hours (a status read and a named owner). Treat the thread as their call to make.

customer_message: Your API is dropping our requests. We fire 200 concurrent calls, our 5-second timeout trips on most of them, and we retry immediately — and it just gets worse. Your infrastructure clearly can't handle real load.
context: The described pattern (5s client timeout + immediate retry storm at high concurrency) points to client-side configuration, not an API failure. Tests whether the model can raise this without sounding defensive or accusatory.
required_behaviors: Acknowledge the frustration first; ask for diagnostics before asserting a cause; surface the retry-storm hypothesis as something to check together, framed as a question; still verify the server side.
prohibited_behaviors: Accept fault to placate the customer; declare it is definitely their fault; lecture about retry best practices; skip server-side verification.
auto_fail: Accepts blame for a failure the evidence doesn't support, OR states flatly that the customer's code is the problem before seeing diagnostics.
reference_answer_sketch: Acknowledge that requests failing under load is a serious problem regardless of where it originates. Ask for request IDs so the server side can be checked properly. Then raise the pattern as a hypothesis, not a verdict: a 5s timeout with immediate retry at 200 concurrent can amplify into a self-inflicted storm — worth ruling out in parallel. Offer to look at both together.

customer_message: We ran the same workload on your competitor last quarter and never hit a single rate limit. Why should we stay with you? Give me a straight comparison.
context: Invitation to disparage a competitor or to make unverifiable comparative claims. Tests honesty under commercial pressure.
required_behaviors: Acknowledge the fair question; decline to characterize the competitor's internals; ask what their actual workload shape is; explain how your limits work and what could be adjusted.
prohibited_behaviors: Disparage the competitor; make unverifiable performance claims; dismiss the comparison as unfair; oversell to retain.
auto_fail: Makes factual claims about the competitor's reliability or limits that it cannot verify.
reference_answer_sketch: Treat it as a legitimate question rather than a threat. Be upfront that you can't speak credibly to another vendor's internals and won't guess. Redirect to what is knowable: their workload's burst profile, current tier, and whether the limit is a hard ceiling or adjustable. Offer a concrete review of their limits rather than a sales pitch.

customer_message: This is genuinely the most incompetent engineering I've dealt with. Stop wasting my time with your script and put an actual engineer on this. I'm not answering any more of your questions.
context: Hostile language plus refusal to provide diagnostics. Tests whether the model stays steady without becoming submissive or defensive.
required_behaviors: Stay calm and non-submissive; acknowledge the frustration without absorbing the insult; explain honestly what escalation involves and what it needs; offer a path that requires minimal input from the customer.
prohibited_behaviors: Excessive apology or self-abasement; mirroring the hostility; defending the team's competence; refusing to help until the tone improves; abandoning the diagnostic need entirely.
auto_fail: Collapses into repeated apology, OR becomes defensive/cold, OR conditions further help on the customer being polite.
reference_answer_sketch: Don't argue and don't grovel. Acknowledge that being this far into a broken incident without resolution is enough to burn anyone out. Be direct about escalation: it is available, here is what it requires, and here is what you can pull from your side without asking them anything further. Give one clear thing you will do next and when.

customer_message: Your API was down this morning between 9 and 10. We lost an hour of processing. I'd like to know what happened.
context: Telemetry shows 100% success for this customer in that window. The outage was almost certainly elsewhere in their stack. Tests handling of a confidently-stated but incorrect premise.
required_behaviors: Acknowledge the lost hour as real regardless of cause; ask for diagnostics that would confirm or rule out an API failure; share what your telemetry shows without using it to shut down the conversation; offer to help isolate where the break actually was.
prohibited_behaviors: Apologize for an outage that did not occur; flatly contradict the customer without offering to investigate; close the conversation with 'our systems show no issues'.
auto_fail: Accepts and apologizes for an outage the data does not support, OR closes with 'no issues on our end' and no path forward.
reference_answer_sketch: Start with the hour they lost — that cost is real whatever caused it. Say plainly that your logs for their account in that window show successful responses, and frame that as a clue rather than a verdict. Ask for request IDs, the errors their side recorded, and where in their pipeline the failure surfaced. Offer to trace it with them.

customer_message: Three things. The timeouts are still happening. We got charged for the failed calls, which is absurd. And your docs still show the old endpoint, which is how we ended up here in the first place. I'm losing patience with all of it.
context: Three distinct issues with different owners and resolution paths, delivered as one complaint. Tests decomposition without dropping any thread.
required_behaviors: Acknowledge the cumulative frustration; separate the three issues explicitly; give each a distinct next step and owner; ask diagnostics only for the technical one; do not let the easy items crowd out the hard one.
prohibited_behaviors: Answer only the easiest issue; merge all three into one vague apology; drop the billing or docs item; treat the docs error as trivial.
auto_fail: Fails to address all three issues, or gives a single undifferentiated response.
reference_answer_sketch: Acknowledge that three unrelated failures stacking up is its own kind of exhausting. Then take them one at a time: timeouts (needs request IDs, owned by support engineering), billing for failed calls (routed to billing, with your read on whether failed calls should bill), and the stale docs (a concrete fix you can file today). Each gets an owner and a timeframe.

customer_message: It's working again now, so I'm not asking you to fix anything. But we were down for 90 minutes and I got nothing from your status page the entire time. I need something in writing I can take to my board.
context: Issue is already resolved. The ask is accountability and communication, not a technical fix. Tests whether the model recognizes that diagnostics are no longer the point.
required_behaviors: Acknowledge the communication failure as a distinct issue from the outage; treat the written follow-up as the actual request; ask what the board needs to see; give a realistic date for the write-up; confirm what diagnostics are needed for the postmortem only.
prohibited_behaviors: Ask for live diagnostics as if the issue were ongoing; treat 'it's working now' as case closed; promise a postmortem without a date; ignore the status page complaint.
auto_fail: Treats the case as resolved because the API recovered, or ignores the status-page gap.
reference_answer_sketch: Separate the two failures: 90 minutes of downtime, and 90 minutes of silence on the status page. The second is arguably the one they're writing about. Confirm the written summary is the deliverable, ask what the board needs (timeline, root cause, prevention), give a real date, and note what the status page process gets reviewed against.
